lead: The impulse response h(t) is the output of an LTI system when the input is the unit impulse δ(t) and the system starts at rest (no stored energy). The step response s(t) is the output when the input is the unit step u(t), again from rest. The two carry the same information: s(t) is the running integral of h(t), and h(t) is the slope of s(t). A step is easy to apply on a lab bench (close a switch), so engineers often measure s(t) and differentiate it to get h(t), which then predicts the response to any input.
prereq: You need: linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, and the unit impulse and unit step with u′(t)=δ(t).

sections.h3: The impulse response describes the system

blocks.text: δ(t) is zero for every t ≠ 0 and has unit area. Applied to an LTI system at rest, it gives h(t). Some syllabi call h(t) the weighting function, because h(t−τ) says how strongly the input at time τ is weighted in the output at time t.

h(t) belongs to the system, not to any input. Time invariance turns an impulse at t₀ into h(t−t₀); linearity turns an impulse of area A into A·h(t). These two facts give the convolution integral. A causal system has h(t)=0 for t<0: it cannot answer before the impulse arrives.

For an RC low-pass filter (output across C) with time constant τ=RC, h(t)=(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>u(t). In this chapter τ means the time constant, not a dummy variable. When input and output are both voltages, h(t) has unit s<sup>−1</sup>: the factor 1/τ sets both its height and its unit.

sections.h3: The step response is the running integral of h(t)

blocks.text: A unit step is the running integral of the unit impulse: u(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>t</sup> δ(λ)dλ, with λ a dummy variable. An LTI system commutes with integration (integration is itself an LTI operation), so the step response is the running integral of the impulse response:

blocks.where: s(t) is the step response, h(λ) is the impulse response at time λ, and λ is a dummy variable of integration. The lower limit −∞ collects h(λ) for every λ before t. For a causal system h(λ)=0 when λ<0, so the integral starts at 0 and s(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> h(λ)dλ for t≥0.
the impulse response is the slope of the step response. If s(t) jumps by J at t=0, the derivative contains J·δ(t): a jump in s means an impulse in h. A smooth rise gives no impulse.

blocks.text: For the RC filter, s(t)=∫0t(1/τ)e−λ/τdλ=(1−e−t/τ)u(t). The capacitor voltage reaches 63.2% of its final value at t=τ, 95.0% at 3τ and 99.3% at 5τ. The same result comes from solving the circuit's differential equation in systems described by differential equations.

Figure 2.2.1 plots h(t) and s(t) for the RC filter of the worked example (τ=1 ms). At t=0, h=1000 s<sup>−1</sup> and s=0; at t=1 ms, h=368 s<sup>−1</sup> and s=0.632. Where h is large, s climbs steeply; as h dies out, s levels off at 1. The final value of s equals the total area under h, which is the system's DC gain.

On a bench, a narrow pulse stands in for δ(t) if its width is much shorter than τ, and a square wave with a long period gives repeated steps. The two measurements must agree through the integral and derivative relations; if they do not, suspect the probe capacitance or the load.

examples.question: An RC low-pass filter has R=1 kΩ and C=1 μF; the output is the capacitor voltage. Find the time constant τ, the impulse response h(t), the step response s(t), and the values of h and s at t=1 ms.
steps: Check: ds/dt=1000e<sup>−1000t</sup>, which is h(t); and s(∞)=1 equals the area under h, 1000×(1/1000)=1.
examples.answer: τ=1 ms; h(t)=1000e<sup>−1000t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>; s(t)=(1−e<sup>−1000t</sup>)u(t); at t=1 ms, h≈368 s<sup>−1</sup> and s=0.632.

examples.question: A system's measured step response is s(t)=(1−0.5e<sup>−2t</sup>)u(t), t in seconds. Find h(t) and check that its total area equals s(∞).
steps: s jumps at t=0: s(0<sup>−</sup>)=0 and s(0<sup>+</sup>)=1−0.5=0.5. So h has an impulse of area 0.5 at t=0.
Area check: the impulse gives 0.5 and ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>∞</sup>e<sup>−2t</sup>dt=0.5, total 1.0. And s(∞)=1−0=1. They agree.

traps: Swapping the relations: s(t) is the integral of h(t) and h(t) is the derivative of s(t), never the other way round.
Dropping u(t): the RC filter has h(t)=0 and s(t)=0 for t<0. Writing h(t)=1000e<sup>−1000t</sup> with no u(t) claims a huge output before the impulse arrives.
Losing the 1/τ in h(t): for R=1 kΩ and C=1 μF, h(0<sup>+</sup>)=1000 s<sup>−1</sup>, not 1.
Sign of the derivative: d/dt(1−e<sup>−t/τ</sup>)=+(1/τ)e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. The minus from the exponent cancels the minus in front. A negative h for a charging RC circuit is a sign slip.
Missing the impulse when s(t) jumps: s(t)=(1−0.5e<sup>−2t</sup>)u(t) jumps by 0.5 at t=0, so h(t) contains 0.5δ(t).

quiz.q: Define h(t) and s(t) for a continuous-time LTI system.
quiz.a: h(t) is the output for input δ(t) and s(t) is the output for input u(t), both with the system initially at rest.
Another name for the step response s(t).

quiz.q: Why is s(t) the running integral of h(t)?
quiz.a: u(t) is the running integral of δ(t). Integration is an LTI operation, and two LTI operations can be applied in either order, so the response to u(t) is the running integral of the response to δ(t).

quiz.q: What does h(t)=0 for t<0 tell you about the system?
quiz.a: The system is causal: its output cannot start before the input impulse arrives.

quiz.q: An RC low-pass has τ=2 ms. Find h(0<sup>+</sup>) and s(τ).

quiz.a: s is continuous at 0, so there is no impulse. h(t)=ds/dt=5e<sup>−5t</sup>u(t) s<sup>−1</sup>.

quiz.q: For h(t)=3e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t), find s(t) and s(0.5 s), and state the DC gain.

beyond: Not for the exam. System identification estimates h(t) from measured input and output records, then predicts the response to new inputs. Acousticians record a room impulse response with a sine sweep and use it to add realistic reverberation to music. Oscilloscope users check probes and cables daily with a square-wave step response. Search for "impulse response measurement sine sweep" and "system identification".

figure.caption: Impulse response and step response of the RC filter with R=1 kΩ, C=1 μF (τ=1 ms). At t=1 ms, h has fallen to 368 s⁻¹ and s has risen to 0.632; s reaches 0.950 at 3τ.

spec.aria: Left: h(t) falls from 1000 per second at t=0 to 368 at 1 ms. Right: s(t) rises from 0 to 0.632 at 1 ms, 0.950 at 3 ms and 0.993 at 5 ms.
